name: Shallot
label: shallot row

planting.note: sets 5 in apart in rows 12 in apart; four rows of a dozen

bed30.note: three rows 9 in apart; sets or transplants, same spacing

watch_for: onion maggot (row cover before the 390 GDD flight, says UMaine), onion thrips in hot dry summers, allium leaf miner — not yet confirmed in Maine but spreading through New England, so scout for its leaf-puncture marks; purple blotch in wet years
watering: Even, consistent moisture while bulbing; stop watering once the tops yellow.
method_notes: A spring-planted cool-season allium: plant sets as soon as the ground can be worked in April, lift when the tops fall over, cure like onions. From seed, start indoors in Feb-Mar and set out early; Fedco's seed shallots run ~105 days and Johnny's ~110. Coleman grows them in the same 30-inch-bed system with tight in-row spacing instead of wide rows.
source: UMaine Extension Planting Chart and 2025-26 UMaine allium IPM newsletters (pest GDD thresholds); New England Vegetable Management Guide (onion/scallion/shallot: transplants 10-12 weeks before setting, 9-18 in rows, 3-4 in in-row); Fedco catalog (Camelot: 4-6 in spacing in beds; Val-aux-Vents 105 days from seed); Johnny's (Innovator 110 days from direct seed, subtract 10-15 if transplanted); Coleman bed system per Johnny's/NOG.

name: Scallion
label: scallion band

planting.note: sown thick in four 2-3 in wide bands; thin to 1-2 in apart

bed30.note: four dense bands (2-3 in wide) across the bed, thinned to an inch apart

watch_for: onion maggot (put row cover on before the 390 GDD emergence UMaine tracks), thrips in hot dry summers, allium leaf miner — scallions are a preferred spring host, so keep spring and fall crops covered if ALM is in your area; re-sow every 3 weeks rather than fighting any of them
watering: Never let the soil dry during germination; steady moisture after that or the stems turn hot and stringy.
method_notes: The easiest winter crop in Coleman's unheated zone-5 houses — one of his ~30 overwintered vegetables. Fedco calls overwintered Evergreen Hardy White 'a welcome treat in April': sow July-August for fall and spring harvest, April for summer. When bolted overwintered plants go to seed, cut the patch back to 2 in and it re-grows tender scallions.
source: Fedco catalog (Evergreen Hardy White, 65 days, overwintering and cut-back advice); Johnny's (65 days from direct seed; sow early spring through early fall, extra-hardy types survive winter in well-drained soil); Univ. of Minnesota Extension scallion guide (direct-sow as soon as soil is workable, thin to 1 in); New England Vegetable Management Guide (2-3 in wide rows, mid-summer plantings for fall); Coleman, The Winter Harvest Handbook (scallions in the winter crop list, zone 5 Maine); UMaine IPM newsletters (maggot/thrips/ALM thresholds).

name: Chives
label: chive edge

planting.note: one row of clumps 12 in apart along the bed edge; it is a permanent border

bed30.note: a single row of clumps 12-18 in apart against the path side

watch_for: Almost nothing — no significant pests or diseases per UW Extension, but two real risks: allium leaf miner prefers chives to any other allium (Cornell trap-crop trials), so a chive clump is the first place to scout in spring, and thrips silver the leaves in hot dry summers. Divide before the clump starves itself.
watering: Drought-tolerant once established; a weekly soak in dry spells keeps the leaves tender.
method_notes: The first green of the spring and a true perennial — one planting serves for years. Plant a clump per 12 in along the edge of a bed, cut back hard after flowering for fresh regrowth, and divide every 2-3 years. Fedco sells it as Maine-grown plants, hardy to zone 3.
source: Fedco catalog (chives: 12-18 in spacing, full to part sun, Z3, Maine Grown, cut back after flowering); UW-Madison Extension 'Chives, Allium schoenoprasum' (no significant pests, divisions every 2-3 years, start seeds a few weeks before last frost); UNH Extension garlic-chives profile (80-90 days, full sun to part shade, Z3); Cornell/ESA allium leafminer host-preference study (chives most preferred); UMaine IPM newsletters (spring ALM generation hits chives first).

name: Walking Onion
label: walking onion patch

planting.note: bulblets 6 in apart in two rows 12 in apart; a permanent patch, divided not replanted

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart; bulblets pressed 1 in deep, 5-6 in apart

watch_for: Thrips in hot dry summers (mostly cosmetic, says UW); allium leaf miner is the real one — a perennial allium patch is exactly where ALM overwinters, so a walking-onion bed can hold the pest for the whole garden: scout for leaf punctures in spring and again in September and cull infested plants
watering: Tough once established; water only in extended drought.
method_notes: A. cepa x A. fistulosum, hardy to zone 3, that 'walks': bulblets form on the stalk top, flop over, and replant themselves yards away. Plant bulblets (or divisions) in fall or spring; eat young shoots as scallions in spring, pull the strong underground bulbs late summer, and replant the topsets. No days-to-maturity is published for it — the 60-90 range is realistic field time from a planted bulblet.
source: UW-Madison Extension (Mahr), 'Egyptian Walking Onions' (hardy zones 3-10, bulblets 1 in deep 4-5 in apart, thrips mostly cosmetic, divide clumps in spring); UF/IFAS EDIS 'Onion, Tree' (rows 12 in apart, plants 3-6 in); Cornell Botanic Gardens profile (A. x proliferum, perennial polycarpic, young plants used as scallions); Territorial Seed culture notes (bulblets 5-6 in apart 1 in deep, underground bulbs late summer to early fall). Not listed in Fedco or Johnny's catalogs — source is extension, not commercial DTM.
